**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference and training workloads

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own before committing to any new purchases. We should treat a purchase decision as a live option we keep open, not one we close, and we should define now the utilisation thresholds that would trigger it. This is not an argument that we will never need more hardware; it is an argument that we do not yet know whether we need more hardware, and that the cheapest way to find out is to measure and manage what we have.

**The case for buying**

The argument for buying more capacity is straightforward and partly correct. Our queue times during the last two sprint retrospectives were real, and a handful of engineers lost meaningful days waiting for a free GPU to run evaluation jobs. Latency to first result matters: when iteration cycles stretch from hours to days, the cost is not just idle salary but lost experiments we never thought to run. There is also a reliability argument. Our current fleet has no meaningful headroom, so a single node failure during a training run forces queue reshuffling that delays other teams. Redundancy is a genuine operational good, and we should not pretend otherwise.

**The case for patience**

But the purchase case rests on an assumption we have not tested: that our hardware is actually saturated. The telemetry we do have suggests otherwise. Our fleet-wide GPU utilisation averages somewhere in the low forties percent, and our own spot checks found jobs allocated to cards while the models sat idle in data loading or waiting on a single-GPU bottleneck in a multi-GPU job. A meaningful fraction of our "capacity shortage" is almost certainly a scheduling and configuration problem wearing a capacity shortage's clothes. Before we spend capital on new cards, we should know whether we are buying compute or buying relief from our own inefficiency.

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and this is where I want to be honest about the trade-off. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on engineering time, and the reverse is also true. But the two options differ sharply in reversibility. Hardware is a largely one-way door: cards depreciate, consume power, take rack space, and cannot be un-bought if our workload mix changes in six months. Utilisation work — better job scheduling, batching improvements, quantisation for inference, moving bursty evaluation jobs to spot cloud capacity — is mostly reversible and, more importantly, generates knowledge. Even if we end up buying hardware later, the utilisation work tells us exactly how much to buy and makes the purchase smaller. The reverse is not true: buying first tells us nothing and locks in the cost.

There is also a latency consideration that favours the utilisation path in the near term. Lead times on high-end accelerators are long, and procurement, budgeting, and installation would mean new hardware is realistically two to three months away even if we approved it tomorrow. Scheduling and batching improvements can start producing results in weeks. If the team is feeling pain now, the faster relief is the one we control ourselves.

**What I am uncertain about**

I want to flag the limits of this recommendation rather than oversell it. First, our utilisation numbers are sparse and possibly unrepresentative; a proper week of instrumentation might reveal that peak-hour contention is worse than averages suggest, and peak-hour contention is exactly what engineers feel even when fleet-wide utilisation is modest. Second, utilisation improvements have a ceiling. If our workload is genuinely growing at the rate the roadmap implies, no amount of scheduling cleverness will defer the purchase indefinitely, and delaying too long converts a planned capital expense into an emergency one, which is the worst of both worlds. Third, there is a real risk that a quarter of "optimisation" work becomes its own opportunity cost, absorbing engineering time that could have gone to product work. We should scope it tightly — two engineers, one quarter, clear exit criteria.

**Proposed next steps**

Concretely: instrument the fleet properly for two weeks, implement queue-based scheduling and batch-size tuning, pilot spot capacity for bursty jobs, and reconvene at the end of the quarter with real numbers. If peak-hour utilisation then exceeds roughly eighty percent with queue times still degrading iteration speed, we buy, and we will buy with confidence and a defensible size estimate rather than a feeling. If utilisation remains low, we will have saved a substantial capital outlay and learned something durable about our own infrastructure.

The purchase will still be there in three months. The chance to understand our own workload before paying for more of it is the thing worth taking now.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've reached the point in the quarter where the question of GPU capacity has come up again, and I want to lay out my thinking before we meet on Thursday. The framing we've been using — "buy more hardware versus improve utilisation" — is a reasonable one, but I think the two options are less symmetrical than they first appear, and the asymmetry should drive our decision.

Let me start with the case that's easiest to make: our current utilisation is genuinely poor. Across the cluster, our scheduling data shows average utilisation in the low thirties, with individual nodes swinging between idle and saturated within the same day. A meaningful fraction of that is structural — batch jobs queued behind interactive workloads, models held resident in memory while waiting for traffic that arrives in bursts, and a development queue that competes with production for the same cards. None of this is mysterious, and none of it is cheap to fix, but the headroom is real. If we lifted average utilisation to even fifty percent through better queueing, time-slicing for the dev fleet, and consolidating the small models that currently each pin their own GPU, we would effectively add capacity equivalent to several new nodes without spending a dollar on hardware.

That said, I want to be honest about the costs of the utilisation path, because they're easy to underestimate. The engineering work is not glamorous and it is not small. Rewriting our scheduler policies, instrumenting per-job cost attribution, and migrating services onto a shared inference layer will consume roughly two engineers for a quarter, and during that period those engineers are not shipping product features. That is the opportunity cost, and it is the strongest argument on the other side of the ledger. There's also a risk that utilisation gains prove harder to capture than the numbers suggest — utilisation measured as GPU-seconds busy is not the same as useful throughput, and some of our "idle" capacity exists precisely because teams value guaranteed latency over efficiency.

Which brings me to latency and reliability, because they cut in different directions. On latency, the utilisation path carries genuine risk: packing workloads more tightly means more contention, more queueing at peak, and tail latencies that depend on neighbours behaving well. For our interactive inference paths, that's a real regression risk, and I don't think we should pretend otherwise. On reliability, though, the picture favours the status quo fleet. Adding new hardware means new nodes to integrate, new failure modes to learn, and a supply chain lead time measured in months — during which our reliability story doesn't improve at all. Squeezing more out of existing hardware, by contrast, means operating equipment we already understand, with known failure rates and spare parts on the shelf.

Then there is reversibility, which I think is the decisive consideration. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale. The capital is spent, depreciation begins, and if demand shifts — because a model gets more efficient, because a product direction changes, because the vendor landscape moves — we own cards we can't easily sell. Improving utilisation is almost entirely reversible. If a scheduling change degrades latency, we roll it back. If a consolidation project stalls, we've lost engineering time but retained optionality. In an environment where model efficiency is improving fast enough that our per-token compute needs have dropped meaningfully twice in the past year, locking in capital now is a bet that our demand forecast beats the efficiency curve. I'm not confident in that bet, and I don't think we should make it with money we could keep in hand.

So my recommendation is this: commit to the utilisation work as the primary path for the next two quarters, with a specific, measurable target — I'd propose raising sustained utilisation above fifty percent while holding p99 inference latency within current bounds — and treat hardware purchase as a contingent decision we revisit at the end of that period. If utilisation gains fall short, or if latency regressions prove unacceptable, we will have learned enough to buy with better information, and the lead time on new hardware is long enough that we can pull the trigger then without falling behind.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My utilisation figures come from our own telemetry, which has known gaps around idle-but-reserved memory, so the true headroom could be smaller than I've suggested. And there's a scenario — a major product launch in Q3 — where demand simply outruns whatever we squeeze out of the current fleet. If that launch is confirmed, I'd revise this recommendation toward a modest hardware order now, precisely because lead times make waiting expensive in that world.

Let's discuss Thursday. My ask is that we agree on the utilisation target and the review date, so that "wait and improve" doesn't quietly become "wait indefinitely."

— Infrastructure Working Group

**MEMO: Compute Capacity — Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering team
**From:** Infra lead
**Re:** Local AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local GPU fleet for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, a couple of recent training runs had to be rescheduled, and the natural instinct in a moment like this is to buy our way out of the problem. Before we do that, I want to lay out why I think the better move — at least for the next quarter — is to invest in utilisation first, with a small, capped hardware purchase as a hedge rather than a first response.

Start with the economics. Our current fleet is roughly 40% idle on average across a 24-hour cycle, and that idle time is not evenly distributed: it clusters overnight and on weekends, exactly when our peak demand is spilling over. Buying more hardware to cover peak load means paying for machines that will sit mostly unused, and GPU pricing has not gotten friendlier. Beyond the capital cost, each additional node carries real carrying costs — power, cooling, rack space, and, less glamorously, the engineering time to image, monitor, and maintain it. We are a small team; every node we add is a node someone has to babysit. Utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly labour we already pay for, applied to assets we already own. The payback period on a scheduling and queueing project is measured in weeks; the payback period on new hardware is measured in years, and only if our demand curve cooperates.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to take it seriously rather than wave it away. Interactive workloads — the notebook-style experimentation most of us do daily — genuinely suffer when the queue is deep. Waiting twenty minutes for a job that takes four to run is a real tax on iteration speed, and iteration speed is where a small team wins or loses. But the fix for latency is not necessarily more capacity; it's better allocation. Right now we have no meaningful priority system, no preemption, and several long-running jobs that monopolise cards while doing I/O for large fractions of their runtime. A proper scheduler with fair sharing and checkpointing would do more for perceived latency than two additional nodes would, because it would attack the variance in wait time rather than the mean. Variance is what makes the queue feel broken.

Reliability cuts both ways, and this is where I feel genuine uncertainty. More hardware means more redundancy: if a node dies mid-run today, we lose the run, and we've had two node failures this quarter. A larger fleet spreads that risk. On the other hand, more nodes means more failure surface, and our current monitoring is thin enough that a third node might just mean a third thing that breaks quietly. I'd rather harden what we have — better health checks, automatic job resubmission, honest capacity dashboards — before we multiply the things that can fail. If we can't reliably operate N nodes, N+1 doesn't make us more reliable; it makes us more optimistic.

The opportunity-cost question is the one I keep returning to. The budget we'd spend on hardware is budget we don't spend on people, tooling, or the product itself. And the utilisation work — scheduling, profiling, right-sizing models to hardware — is work that pays off regardless of how big the fleet eventually gets. If we buy hardware first and the demand spike turns out to be a two-month anomaly tied to one project, we've made an irreversible-ish bet on a temporary problem. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are largely reversible and compounding: a scheduler we build this quarter still helps us in three years, and if demand keeps growing, we'll buy hardware then, with better data about what we actually need and with the new nodes landing into a system that can absorb them efficiently.

That said, I don't want to pretend this is cost-free. Utilisation work takes engineer-weeks we'd otherwise spend on features, and it has a real risk of becoming a yak-shave — scheduler projects have a way of growing scope. There's also a chance that our demand is genuinely structural, not cyclical, in which case we're delaying the inevitable. To hedge both risks, I propose a modest, pre-approved hardware budget — one additional node, not a fleet expansion — held in reserve and triggered only if utilisation work stalls or if demand keeps climbing after the scheduling changes land. That keeps the option open without committing us to it by default.

My recommendation, then: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — queueing, profiling, and monitoring — before any significant purchase, with a small capped hardware option as insurance. Measure wait-time percentiles before and after so we're arguing from data next time. If we're still saturated in April, we buy, and we'll buy smarter for having waited.

Happy to argue about this in Thursday's eng meeting.
